zoom.label: The angel: its face turned out of the picture and its pointing right hand

c1.text: Level one: Leonardo changed this angel's pose. Now look closely: its eyes and its finger aim in two different directions.

zoom.label: The angel: its face turned out of the picture and its pointing right hand

c1q.text: Who is the angel's finger pointing at?

sources.title: National Gallery, London, NG1093, The Virgin of the Rocks (collection page)
Colette Féraudet, 'La Vierge aux rochers', Panorama de l'art (Rmn-Grand Palais), 27 Mar 2023
Louvre collection record, INV 777, La Vierge aux rochers (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)

c1m.text: Eyes on you, finger on John: Leonardo's rethought angel links you to the scene.

c1a.text: Yes. The angel's eyes look out at you, but its finger points across the group to John, the baby Mary draws in with her arm.

c1b.text: Close: Jesus sits beside the angel, but he isn't the target.

correction.tempting: Jesus sits right by the angel, who steadies him, so the hand seems to belong to him.
correction.truth: The finger points away from Jesus, across to John, the kneeling baby Jesus is blessing.
correction.evidence: National Gallery and Grand Palais: the Paris angel points to Saint John the Baptist. The Louvre: Jesus blesses his cousin.

c1c.text: Half right: the eyes are for you, the finger isn't.

correction.tempting: The angel turns and looks straight out at you, so the gesture feels addressed to you.
correction.truth: Its gaze is on you; its finger points across the group to John.
correction.evidence: The National Gallery: in the Paris version the angel "looks out at us and points towards Saint John the Baptist".

zoom.label: Mary's head and the dark space above it, with no halo

c2.text: Level one: Paris came first and London followed. Look at the space just above Mary's head. London's twin does something different here.

zoom.label: Mary's head and the dark space above it, with no halo

c2q.text: What does London's version add above her head?

sources.title: National Gallery, London, NG1093, The Virgin of the Rocks (collection page)
National Gallery, London, 'Leonardo: Experience a Masterpiece' (2019), The lost altarpiece
Louvre collection record, INV 777, La Vierge aux rochers (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)
Colette Féraudet, 'La Vierge aux rochers', Panorama de l'art (Rmn-Grand Palais), 27 Mar 2023
L. Keith, A. Roy, R. Morrison, P. Schade, 'Leonardo da Vinci's Virgin of the Rocks: Treatment, Technique and Display', National Gallery Technical Bulletin 32 (2011)

c2m.text: London adds halos, John's cross and bigger figures; Paris, the first version, leaves its heads bare.

c2a.text: Yes. In London all but the angel wear the thinnest gold rings as halos. Here in Paris, look again: her head is bare.

c2b.text: London does add a cross, just not up here.

correction.tempting: London's John carries a gilded cross, so a golden addition near her head sounds right.
correction.truth: London's cross is tucked under John's arm. Above her head, London adds a thin gold halo.
correction.evidence: National Gallery: John carries "a gilded cross under his arm", and the figures wear "the thinnest of gold rings as halos".

correction.tempting: The London picture feels roomier and lighter, so you might expect more sky.
correction.truth: London cuts down the sky at the top, so the figures look bigger and closer.
correction.evidence: National Gallery: London's figures "appear bigger and closer" after cutting down the sky. Grand Palais: "les figures sont plus grandes".

zoom.label: Mary's raised left hand above the baby Jesus

c3.text: In level one you may have spotted Mary's left hand, floating above the baby on the right, fingers spread. Here it is up close.

zoom.label: Mary's raised left hand above the baby Jesus

c3q.text: What is Mary's raised hand doing?

sources.title: Louvre collection record, INV 777, La Vierge aux rochers (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)
Colette Féraudet, 'La Vierge aux rochers', Panorama de l'art (Rmn-Grand Palais), 27 Mar 2023
National Gallery, London, NG1093, The Virgin of the Rocks (collection page)
National Gallery, London, NG6337, The Burlington House Cartoon

c3m.text: One hand draws John in, the other shields Jesus: Mary gathers both children.

c3a.text: Yes. The Louvre says her hand, reaching towards her son, seems meant to protect him; the Grand Palais says Mary protects Jesus with her left hand.

c3b.text: Someone blesses here, but not Mary.

correction.tempting: Raised hands often bless in religious pictures, and a blessing really is happening in this scene.
correction.truth: The blessing comes from Jesus, raising his hand towards John. Mary's hand hovers over Jesus, protecting him.
correction.evidence: The Louvre: the Child "bénit son cousin". The National Gallery: his right hand is raised "in a blessing motion towards John".

c3c.text: A Leonardo gesture, but not this one.

correction.tempting: Leonardo loved pointing hands: the angel points here, and Saint Anne points upward in his London cartoon.
correction.truth: Mary's hand doesn't point; its open palm hovers over Jesus's head, as if to shield him.
correction.evidence: Grand Palais: Mary protects Jesus with her left hand, "posée au-dessus de sa tête". National Gallery: "palm down, in a protective gesture".

extends.concept: The angel's changed pose; who's who; gaze versus gesture

c1q.what_you_learn: The angel's gaze and finger do different jobs: eyes on the viewer, finger on John; and which baby is which.
